title: The city was asleep.
paragraphs: The noise faded. The market voices disappeared. The temple courts emptied. The religious performances quieted. And somewhere between the flickering oil lamps and the cold stone streets… a Pharisee walked through the darkness carrying questions he could no longer silence.
A man everyone assumed was already close to God.
And Scripture says he came to Jesus “by night.”
But the night was not random.
Because this was not just a secret meeting.
This was the beginning of a man’s internal collapse.
“Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night…”
In the original Greek, the phrase is:

“ἦλθεν πρὸς αὐτὸν νυκτός”
(ēlthen pros auton nyktos)

Literally:
“He came to Him in the night.”
But in the Gospel of John, darkness is rarely just physical darkness.
John constantly uses light and darkness symbolically.

“καὶ τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει”
“And the Light shines in the darkness.”
Nicodemus was not merely walking through nighttime Jerusalem.
He was walking through spiritual darkness while standing inches away from the Light of the World.
And maybe that is why this story still hurts so deeply today.
Because some of the darkest people are not the openly rebellious.
Sometimes they are the deeply religious.

People who know Scripture…
but do not know God.

People who mastered theology…
but never surrendered their hearts.

People applauded publicly…
while privately suffocating spiritually.
He belonged to the Pharisees — the strictest religious movement in Judaism at the time. The Hebrew root connected to “Pharisee” comes from “פָּרַשׁ” (parash), meaning “to separate.”

But somewhere along the way…
they also separated themselves from humility.
He probably had massive portions of Torah memorized in Hebrew.

And yet when he stood before Jesus…
he sounded spiritually starving.
There is something devastating about realizing information cannot save you.

You can know verses…
and still not know peace.

You can preach…
and still be empty.

You can lead others spiritually…
while quietly dying inside.

And maybe…
that is some of us.
“Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher come from God…”
Others were disturbed by Him too.
Others secretly knew something supernatural was happening.
Only Nicodemus walked into the dark searching for answers.
And before Nicodemus can even finish his speech…
Jesus cuts directly into the wound.
“Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.”

“ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν”
(ean mē tis gennēthē anōthen)
Jesus intentionally uses a word layered with spiritual depth.
And suddenly the greatest religious mind in the room is confused.
“How can a man be born when he is old?”
And this shattered Nicodemus because Pharisees believed righteousness was achieved through strict obedience.

But Jesus was saying:
“You cannot polish your dead soul enough to enter God’s kingdom.”
That truth still offends religious pride today.
We love controlling our own salvation story.
“All our righteousnesses are as filthy rags.”

The Hebrew phrase for “filthy rags” is shockingly graphic:
“בֶּגֶד עִדִּים”
(beged iddim)
Human righteousness before God is not impressive.
And Nicodemus — the elite teacher — was hearing this from a carpenter’s Son standing in the dark.
Then Jesus says something even more mysterious:

“τὸ πνεῦμα ὅπου θέλει πνεῖ”
(to pneuma hopou thelei pnei)

The word “πνεῦμα” (pneuma) means:
wind,
breath,
or spirit.
Jesus is describing the Holy Spirit as uncontrollable, sovereign, living, moving.
You cannot engineer salvation through rituals.
The Spirit of God moves beyond human control.
Because Jesus was dismantling the entire illusion that religious status equals spiritual life.
Then comes one of the most heartbreaking moments in the conversation.
“Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?”

In Greek:
“ὁ διδάσκαλος τοῦ Ἰσραήλ”
(ho didaskalos tou Israēl)
Nicodemus was likely one of the highest theological minds in Jerusalem.
And yet he missed the entire point of Scripture.
Because Scripture was always pointing to Christ.
Jesus did not come to make bad people slightly nicer.
He came to raise spiritually dead people back to life.

And then…
in the middle of the night…
Jesus says the verse that would echo across human history forever.

“Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν κόσμον”
(Houtōs gar ēgapēsen ho Theos ton kosmon)
The word “κόσμον” (kosmon) means world — not merely Israel.

And the word used for love is:
“ἠγάπησεν” (ēgapēsen)
A self-giving love that acts for the salvation of the undeserving.
Because many religious leaders believed God’s favor belonged primarily to the righteous.

But Jesus revealed the heart of the Father:
God moves toward sinners.
And maybe this is the untold reason Nicodemus came at night.
Because darkness feels safer when you are falling apart internally.
People hide in darkness when they fear exposure.
Some of you reading this know exactly what that feels like.

You worship publicly…
but secretly feel spiritually numb.

You know Christian language…
but feel distant from God.

You smile in church…
while carrying silent exhaustion.

You post Bible verses…
while privately battling sin, fear, shame, addiction, or unbelief.
And the terrifying part is this:
Religion can hide deadness incredibly well.
Nicodemus teaches us that you can sit inches away from truth for years and still avoid surrender.
But here is the beautiful part.
Jesus did not humiliate Nicodemus for coming in darkness.
Jesus could have exposed him publicly.
Because Christ specializes in meeting broken people in hidden places.
And Nicodemus did not leave unchanged.
Later he cautiously defends Jesus before hostile Pharisees in John 7.
“Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night…”
Because the man who once hid in darkness was now publicly identifying himself with a crucified Christ.
And he brought approximately seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes for Jesus’ burial.
This was no longer secret curiosity.
The Pharisee who once came trembling in darkness was now honoring Jesus openly after the cross.
Jesus was not merely winning an argument in John 3.
And maybe someone reading this feels exactly like Nicodemus tonight.

Close to Scripture…
but far from intimacy with God.
You do not need a better religious mask.

Jesus did not say:
“Improve yourself enough.”

He said:
“You must be born from above.”
Even for people hiding in darkness.
Especially for people hiding in darkness.

Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Send this to someone who looks spiritually strong on the outside but may secretly be struggling internally.

Some people are not running from Jesus in the dark…
they are searching for Him there.
